author: Owen Marsden-Readford
title: Transportation in Sydney is highway robbery
content:
Sydneysiders pay, on average,

more than 15 percent of their income

 just getting around the city week-to-week. It’s a scam that hits working-class residents hardest.

On one hand, there’s the broken public transport system. According to Deutsche Bank’s

Mapping the World’s Prices

 report

, which compares prices across 69 world cities, Sydney’s public transport is the second most expensive in the world, with residents paying up to $2,600 per year in fares. On top of that, the government pays billions to private companies that provide many of the services. The Greater Sydney Bus contract is worth nearly $8 billion, while a private contractor is being paid nearly $4 billion to operate the Metro. So workers pay twice to fund this corporate gravy train—first with their Opal card and again in taxes to fund the companies that profit from running the services.

Yet while costs have soared, the services have gotten worse. Private companies, for example, operate all bus services in the metro area. But the routes are often disrupted, with reduced services and poorer pay and conditions for drivers. The buses are often crowded, if they even show up. In 2023, the ABC

revealed

 that Sydney’s bus contractors were earning bonuses by cancelling thousands of services to meet “on time” targets. “Ghost buses”—ones scheduled to arrive but never do—are common.

The city’s outer suburbs are the least well-served. A 2024

Bus Industry Taskforce report

 found that 235 bus routes failed to meet “minimum service standards”. Most of the routes are in western Sydney. The report said the government needed to invest $10 billion in the coming decades to fix the network.

It is no better for those driving their cars: Sydneysiders pay more than $1 billion in road tolls annually. The city’s thirteen major toll roads are often unavoidable. Transurban, the main company involved, is one of many corporate leeches growing fat off public assets. Many major Transurban toll roads feature locked-in annual price increases of 4 percent or the rate of inflation (whichever is higher), ensuring continuous price hikes for drivers. ​

The state Labor government introduced a $50-per-week toll cap in the latest budget, but it is inadequate. Drivers still pay up to $2,600 per year so that Transurban shareholders can enrich themselves. The cap also leaves the toll road racket untouched. Rather than ending the flow of money to Transurban, the government simply reimburses motorists after they have paid tolls out of pocket. The whole system is highway robbery.

​The first steps to solving the problems are abolishing road tolls, and bringing public transport back into public hands and making it free. Workers should not have to pay for the “privilege” of getting around our own city.

But these measures should only be the beginning. For decades, the city has been designed to make people dependent on cars. The destruction of Sydney’s extensive tram network in the 1950s was one part of this. But more cars and roads relative to trains and trams made congestion worse as the city expanded. A massive investment in public transport infrastructure is needed to reshape Sydney in the interests of working-class residents.

author: Pip Hinman
title: ACTU suggests new plan to boost public housing, reduce rents
content:
The crisis of affordable and secure housing is widely seen as the number one problem facing Australians.

Opinion polls confirm that the cost and availability of affordable and quality housing is at the front of people’s minds. There is a generational pessimism that young people will never own their own home.

Everybody’s Home has found that renting a unit now costs more than half the median take-home pay of a single worker in every capital city. It said that even those on six-figure incomes face rents that exceed 30% of their income. To pay the national median rent, someone on $40,000 would need to spend 89% of their income. For those on $70,000, it’s 56%; for those on $100,000, it’s 41% and for those on $130,000, it’s 33%.

Since the group’s last annual Priced Out report, renters have to find an extra $48 a week — nearly $2500 a year — to cover the national median rent.

While this is being widely reported, so too are scare campaigns in response to the federal government’s modest reforms to negative gearing and capital gains tax (CGT).

A widely aired suggestion, following a report from National Australia Bank and the Ray White real estate group, that landlords would have to lift rents by 30% to compensate for the tax changes, has been found to be a concoction. As Media Watch pointed out on August 24, both groups had predicted a combination of some rent rises and some falls in property prices — which have started to happen since the tax changes.

Meanwhile, the campaign to combat the great rental rip-off and defend the dwindling public housing sector continues.

The Australian Council of Trade Unions (ACTU) has sent a working proposal to the federal Labor government to substantially increase the construction of public housing and set the standard private rental lease period at two years.

The ACTU is calling for one in 10 new homes to be public housing — a five fold rise from present, where just one in 50 new homes being built is public housing. It is also calling for the overall level of public housing to rise to at least 6% of total housing stock.

Action for Public Housing and Campaign for Accessible and Maintained Public Housing, which are campaigning to save the Waterloo Estate from demolition, have supported the ACTU’s initiative and called on Unions NSW to push for more public housing in NSW. They said the ACTU’s plan, if actioned, would “deliver housing security for workers”.

Clearly, the ACTU plan recognises the widespread pain, as a result of insecure housing, but also the growing inequality between generations.

ACTU President Michele O’Neil said Australia once built public housing “at a scale that matched working people’s needs”. She pointed to the Bob Hawke government period in which one in 10 new homes was public housing. She said a government that is serious about fixing the housing crisis would lift the public housing stock “to free up homes in the private rental market and make renting more affordable for everyone”.

The federal treasurer’s dismissive “We’ve already got our plan” response highlights the challenges ahead.

The necessary alliances between the workers’ movement and communities concerned about housing as a human right need to grow into something a lot more powerful.

Green Left believes the right to a secure and quality home is a basic human right. No-one can function without a roof over their heads and as Australia is a rich country, it is not so much a question of resources as politics. We will continue to campaign for the massive expansion of public housing, so that any worker who wants it can get into it — for perpetuity. You can help by becoming a supporter.

author: Tom Sullivan
title: The Spanish Revolution: drawing lessons from defeat
content:
Spain in the 1930s was ripe for revolution. In 1931, generals transitioned the country from military rule to democracy. However, a Popular Front coalition of the Socialist, Communist and liberal Republican parties, and after that a violently repressive far-right government, failed to halt the rising class struggle.

Within the workers’ movement, the dominant force was the National Confederation of Labour (CNT), an anarcho-syndicalist union confederation, explicitly committed to the revolutionary overthrow of capitalism. There were multiple tendencies within the CNT. One of the most important was the Iberian Anarchist Federation (FAI), which formed in 1927 as the self-declared radical anarchists committed to revolution in opposition to a perceived reformist trend in the CNT.

In February 1936, the Popular Front returned to power. The CNT leadership correctly predicted that the military would launch a coup in response and began preparations to resist. On 17 July, the coup began in Spanish Morocco. That same day, FAI members leafleted factory gates with a flyer reading: “The fascist danger, at this moment, is no longer a threat, but a bloody reality...This is no longer the time to hesitate”. The next day, the CNT declared a “revolutionary general strike”. Millions of workers participated.

In Barcelona, CNT defence committees emerged to lead the resistance. These were small groups of experienced militants, some having existed for years, operating in their local neighbourhoods. Since the February elections, they had been preparing for this very moment. Just hours after ringing the factory sirens (the agreed signal the rebellion had begun) they were guarding barricades throughout the city. A few days later, a mass uprising had defeated the fascist rebellion in Barcelona, Madrid and other key cities.

But the workers did not stop at defensive measures. Without any instructions from their leaders, they began collectivising their workplaces. Metalworkers, for example, furnished thick metal sheets onto requisitioned trucks to convert them into armoured vehicles. The nature of production changed overnight, as the transport union explained: “We do not speak of profits— since after deducting staff wages, repair costs and a small reserve fund, the surplus will be handed over to the people for the support of other organisations that may be in need”.

Revolutionary elan took over. Long queues formed outside offices to enlist in workers’ militias. The railway union reported that hundreds of its members had signed up within a fortnight. The General Motors factory sent its first contingent to the front soon after.

In the working-class districts of Barcelona, revolutionary neighbourhood committees formed, often expansions of the defence committees. They converted hotels into communal kitchens, enforced price caps, established militias to patrol the streets, collected taxes, set up schools, expropriated stores and distributed their products, and formed revolutionary tribunals. In some areas, money was briefly replaced by a voucher system administered by the committees. In countless Catalan towns, similar committees formed. In many areas, the local government fled, leaving them as the sole authority.

In other major cities, the collapse of the state was not as deep as in Barcelona, but the workers’ organisations could still exert control. A police officer’s report from Madrid, where the police returned to duty after a few days, shows how this played out. In the report, he recounts his interaction with a militia leader conducting a property search:

“I told him categorically that we were not leaving, as we had to be present for all proceedings carried out there, and by doing so, we were fulfilling the orders of the Director of Security and the Minister of the Interior. He replied that those gentlemen were nobody to them and that if they had to take anyone into custody, they would do so over the Police, the Director, and the Minister.”

The police withdrew.

The July days are often described as “spontaneous.” Although there is always an element of spontaneity in any mass movement, the driving force on the ground was the thousands of hardened CNT militants with years of experience, who were following plans drawn up weeks or months earlier. These pre-existing networks, which included groups of dozens or hundreds of members in the biggest workplaces, were what allowed the revolution to move so quickly from the defensive actions of defeating …

author: Susan Price
title: India: Students force gov’t to cancel corrupt public service exams in Jharkhand
content:
Following ongoing protests by students in India’s Jharkhand state, the state government announced on August 17 the cancellation of the state public service recruitment exam for graduates and all recruitment tests conducted by an outsourced agency, TDPL, in the past 12 years.

The government also announced an investigation into corruption and irregularities in all recruitment examinations conducted in the state since 2014.

Members of the Communist Party of India (Marxist-Leninist) Liberation (CPIML) have been prominent in the struggle against corruption in the education system in India, and played a significant role in the movement in Jharkhand and recent protests in Delhi that resulted in the resignation of the country’s education minister.

The CPIML’s publication ML Update reported: “The student movement [in Jharkhand] began on July 25, following the declaration of the preliminary results of the public service exam. Thousands of students and job aspirants gathered at Jaipal Singh Munda Stadium in Ranchi, raising their demands against irregularities and lack of transparency in the recruitment process.

“The protest was sustained through determined forms of struggle, including a 16-day-long hunger strike by various youth leaders, which further intensified pressure on the government and highlighted the seriousness of the demands raised by students and job aspirants.”

The All India Students Association, Revolutionary Youth Association and other left and progressive student and youth groups organised a massive demonstration, on August 7, near the Jharkhand Assembly, ML Update reported.

“Another massive march was held on August 10, when thousands of students and job aspirants marched through Ranchi towards the Jharkhand Assembly. The protesting youth were met with brutal police violence, including a massive lathi [baton]-charge near the Jharkhand Assembly on the evening of August 10.”

CPIML Jharkhand State Secretary Manoj Bhakt said activists continuously pressured the government to ensure transparency and fairness in the state examination system. Bhakt demanded that the government immediately issue requisitions for new posts within the state public service and release recruitment notifications without further delay.

Bhakt said the government must listen to the questions being raised from schools across Jharkhand about issues of drinking water, clean toilets, playgrounds and the shortage of teachers, which continue to affect students. The entire education system, from primary education to higher education, needs urgent repair and restructuring.

Bakht said “The Modi government must understand that the taxes collected from Jharkhand cannot be meant only for the benefit of Adani and Ambani. They must also serve the people of Jharkhand by ensuring education, employment and a better public system.

“The education system in Jharkhand is in a state of deep crisis and the government must take full responsibility for correcting it. Students must be guaranteed quality education, dignified opportunities, a transparent system and dignified employment.”

author: Joe Allen
title: ‘Mortal danger’: French firefighters battling wildfires and the government
content:
Successive heatwaves across Western Europe through May, June, July and August have propelled one of the biggest wildfire crises the continent has ever seen. Extreme dryness and drought, combined with the most severe, prolonged heat ever experienced, created the conditions for Australian-style bushfires in several countries.

France was hit particularly hard, with temperatures reaching 44 degrees in the south-west. Hundreds of fires spread throughout the country in July and August, forcing hundreds of thousands of people to evacuate their homes, and straining emergency services, which were incapable of dealing with the firestorms and ill-equipped for the extreme conditions.

Joe Allen

, a US-based socialist and author, spoke to French firefighter and trade unionist

Sébastien Delavoux

 about the situation and the political fallout as firefighters demand more resources.

Can you briefly introduce yourself to our readers and describe the working conditions over the last two months?

I am a trade unionist with the CGT (General Confederation of Labour), the second-largest trade union in the country and the second-largest among firefighters, defending the interests of fire and rescue service personnel. I am 48 years old. I have been a firefighter for 32 years, and it has been my profession for 27 years.

For some time now, I have been confined to representing my colleagues in the union, but I have field agents on the phone every day, and I work in a rescue centre. Since 13 July, it has been very intense: every day, contacts with journalists to answer their questions or find them an interlocutor to give testimony.

The fires in Europe received extensive media coverage in the United States, but without in-depth analysis or historical context. Can you describe how terrible this situation was for civilians and firefighters? This was not a sudden event.

Indeed, this is not a sudden or unforeseen phenomenon; scientists have been warning us for decades. As of 22 August, 160,000 hectares have burned, 450 houses have been destroyed, four firefighters have died in the line of duty, and firefighters have lost 30 vehicles destroyed by fire or accident. At the height of the fires in late July, 72 fire brigades (more than 7,200 personnel) were deployed, which is unprecedented. Even so, this was insufficient, as urban vehicles were ill-suited to fighting forest fires in the middle of the forest! Hundreds of thousands of people, residents and tourists alike, have been evacuated.

Since 1973, seventeen forest fires have exceeded 5,000 hectares, including six since 2021; this is the reality of the global warming we were told about, and we are not ready.

How have French firefighters and public sector unions reacted to the fire crisis? Some media outlets are reporting a planned national strike to demand more resources and concrete measures from the Macron government.

Before the fires, in an inter-union group comprising the nine representative trade union organisations, we challenged the prime minister (in April) and met with members of his cabinet on 27 May to tell him that the Civil Security service [the agency responsible for coordinating national emergency responses and disaster relief] is completely inadequate! 

We need to increase the budgets of fire and rescue services, increase the number of professionals, increase the number of vehicles, rethink the organisation of Civil Security and establish a real strategy for this public service.

What was the physical and mental impact of the fire crisis on French firefighters?

Fatigue and fear: facing 40-metre flames in unbearable temperatures is not done without fear, and that’s natural. Forest fire operations are very physically demanding; we sleep little, and we work day and night.

The European and international scale of the fire crisis requires better coordination between firefighters’ unions. Have any political initiatives been taken in this regard?

This year in particular, many countries have been affected: France, Portugal, Spain, Greece; thousands of hectares burned, many houses destroyed, deaths including firefighters.

Each country needs to increase its human and material resources because we need to prepare for major fires occurring simultaneously in several European countries. We must have the means to protect the inhabitants without exposing firefighters to mortal danger to extinguish forest fires.

Are there any upcoming actions by your union?

To force the government to …

author: Kelly Cvetkova
title: Why One Nation is attacking women
content:
Pauline Hanson has spat in the faces of the millions of Australian women who have experienced family violence by describing the crime as a “two-way street”. Returning to a tired victim-blaming rhetoric that women just “shouldn’t put up with it”, she’s trying to turn the clock back on attitudes to women experiencing violence and the real difficulties they face getting support. 

Hanson has featured on right-wing podcasts asserting that women are treating the family courts and child support payments as a “cash cow”, a system that needs to be “reined in”. These comments not only fly in the face of reality but are also an attack on some of the poorest and most vulnerable people in Australia. The 2025 Household, Income and Labour Dynamics survey found that 34.7 percent of children in single parent households live in poverty. Eight out of every ten of these households are headed by women. Domestic abuse is the main reason women become homeless in Australia, women and children making up nine out of the ten people attempting to access specialist housing services. 

Hanson’s outbursts are not the result of ignorance. One Nation’s increased attacks against the rights of women, whether on the issues of domestic abuse, abortion rights or parental leave, are part of the intensification of its far-right agenda, and an attempt to integrate a broader range of social issues into it. Women, according to this logic, are just another interest group that gets “special treatment” thanks to wokeism and whose endless demands are a drain on business and wealth creation. In her now infamous speech at the National Press Club, Hanson made this clear, stating “if women take time off [to have children] and they are not paid their wages because they’re not working, fair enough ... Why should business pay? They’re not at work”.

This parallels her attacks on organisations like the National Indigenous Australians Agency, which she argues should be abolished to save taxpayers from “wasteful Indigenous grants”. She likewise attacks LGBTI people, specifically the “transgender insurgency”, that has “penetrated almost every regulatory authority”. Who is on the other side of this equation?  Apparently, as Hanson told parliament in 2023, “the most oppressed and neglected minority in Australia”, is—wait for it—“men”. 

The positioning around women’s rights is also intended to garner One Nation stronger support with a wider and more hardcore base of potential members and campaigners, most recently on the issue of abortion.

While the party has always maintained sexist talking points about the family courts and the evils of feminism, it has not previously actively campaigned against abortion rights. Hanson has been testing the waters on this issue lately though, indicating that she thinks Australia needs to “have a conversation” about abortion and flagging that she thinks abortion rights should be restricted after twenty weeks. She’s rubbed shoulders with the likes of infamous anti-abortion activist and influencer Joanna Howe. When Malcolm Roberts was questioned at a Brisbane Christian conference about whether the party would move to a policy of banning abortion altogether, the One Nation senator said that it was “becoming [his] goal” to do so.

Barnaby Joyce has been the most explicit in why the change of approach has come now. Speaking to a Sydney crowd of anti-abortion demonstrators, he stated, “What I see before me here is about 1,500 people who can hand out how to vote cards”. One Nation has a clear desire to recruit those sections of the right who are motivated by this issue. And why not—they are an already organised layer of activists who can be relatively easily deployed to campaign, especially if One Nation seems able to deliver and potentially reverse their flagging fortunes. 

Abortion has, in practice, been a settled issue in Australian politics for decades. Nearly three in every four people support legal abortion in some or all cases. But the right know both that there is a motivated minority available to them, and are confident that an aggressive campaign can swing more people behind the cause—especially when Labor is too cowardly to fight on the issue, as it was during the Voice referendum, for example. And the reality is that attitudes to abortion are already going backwards. A

Guardian

 Essential poll found that between November 2024 and July 2026, the percentage of people who agree abortion should be legal in all cases dropped from 41 to …

author: Unknown
title: Üretici, kuru üzüm fiyatının 150 lira olmasını istiyor: “Bu fiyatlarla üreticinin ayakta kalması mümkün değil”
content:
Manisa’nın Alaşehir ilçesinde üzüm hasadının başlamasıyla birlikte üreticilerin artan maliyetler ve düşük alım fiyatları nedeniyle yaşadığı sorunlar yeniden gündeme geldi. Üreticiler mazot, gübre, ilaç, elektrik ve işçilik maliyetlerinin ciddi oranda arttığını, buna karşın üzüm fiyatlarının geçen yılın gerisine düştüğünü belirterek tepki gösterdi.

Maliyetlerin geçen yıla göre önemli ölçüde arttığını ifade eden üzüm üreticisi, mazot dışındaki birçok girdide artışın yüzde 50 seviyesine ulaştığını belirterek, şöyle konuştu:

“İlaçtır, gübredir, işçiliktir, hepsi yüzde 50 artışa geçti. Fakat bizim üzüm neredeyse yüzde 50 düşüşe geçti. Burada para kazanmak mümkün değil artık. Bu da emek. Yetiştirmişiz, mecbur getireceğiz, yapacağız. Yapacak bir şey yok.”

Üretici, düşük fiyatların devam etmesi halinde bağların sökülmesinin gündeme gelebileceğini ancak bunun da çözüm olmadığını söyledi.

Geçen yılki fiyatların enflasyon oranında güncellenmesi gerektiğini ifade eden üretici, “Iskarta üzümü geçen sene 18 liradan sattığın yerde yüzde 80 enflasyonu ekleyeceksiniz bunun üzerine. Olması gereken bu. Kuru üzümün 150 lira olması lazım” dedi.

Çiftçiler Sendikası Denetleme Kurulu Üyesi Gürcan Ertürk ise üzüm hasadının başladığı bu dönemde üreticilerin yüksek maliyetler nedeniyle zor durumda olduğunu söyledi.

Ertürk, “Bu dönem üzüm hasat dönemi. Bağ bozumunun başladığı bir dönem. Fakat maliyetlerinin yüksekliğinden üreticiler çok zor durumda. İlaç maliyetleri, işçi maliyetleri, mazot maliyetleri, giderlerimiz, elektrik maliyetleri çok fazla yüksek olduğu için geçen yıllardaki fiyatları arar olduk” dedi.

Geçen yıllarda 115-120 liraya satılan kuru üzümün bugün 70-75 lira seviyelerinde olduğunu belirten Ertürk, "Burası Alaşehir’in Örnekköy Mahallesi. Şu köyün elektriği var, suyu var, kanalizasyonu var. Her şeyi olmasına rağmen bu köyde insanlar üzümden karnını doyuramadığı için köydeki insanlar çocuklarını büyük şehirlere kendilerine atmış durumda. Köy atıl durumda kalmıştır” diye konuştu.

Üzümün alım fiyatının üreticiyi karşı karşıya bıraktığı tabloya dikkat çeken Ertürk, ıskarta üzümün 10 liraya alındığını belirterek, “Şu üzüm, şu üzüm benim burada ıskartacı alıyor 10 liraya. Geçen sene bu üzüm 18, 20, 22 bandındaydı. Şu anda yaş üzüm 18 ile 25 lira arasında değişiyor” dedi.

Devlet desteğinin artırılması gerektiğini savunan Ertürk, kooperatiflerin ve devletin üreticinin yanında olması gerektiğini belirterek, “Üzümün 150 liradan aşağı olmaması lazım. 150 liraya satılmalı ki vatandaşın derdine bir derman olsun. Bu fiyatlarla üzüm üreticisi ne çocuk okutur ne düğün yapabilir ne sünnet yapar ne de kış geçer" ifadelerini kullandı.

Saruhanlı’nın Dilek Mahallesi’nden üzüm üreticisi Zeki Aytekin ise çektiği video ile yetkililere seslendi. Üzüm fiyatlarına tepki gösteren Aytekin, yaşanan ekonomik sıkıntının üreticiyi bağlarını sökme noktasına getirdiğini söyledi.

Aytekin, “Üzümle birlikte biz de kendimizi toprağa gömdük. Bu düzen böyle gitmez. 75 liraya üzüm alan insanlara vicdansızlıktan başka hiçbir şey demiyorum. Üzümün hali bu. Kara toprak” ifadelerini kullandı.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: CMI Argentina
title: Entre las propiedades que saca a remate, Milei quiere vender el edificio del INAP el organismo destinado a la formación y capacitación de estatales
content:
El Gobierno Nacional puso a la venta el edificio del INAP, el organismo destinado a la formación y capacitación de estatales. Desde ATE Capital rechazaron la propuesta y acusaron a la gestión de querer hacer “negocios inmobiliarios a costa de la formación de los trabajadores del Estado”.


A través del Decreto 764/2026 publicado en el Boletín Oficial el Gobierno Nacional puso a la venta el edificio del Instituto Nacional de la Administración Pública (INAP). Se trata del inmueble que se utiliza para la formación y la capacitación de los trabajadores del Estado.


Desde ATE Capital rechazaron la determinación y acusaron al Gobierno de Javier Milei de realizar “Negocios inmobiliarios a costa de la formación de los trabajadores y trabajadoras del Estado”.


Sito en Av. Belgrano 637, el edificio del INAP que ahora está a la venta fue la sede en la que se realizaron, por ejemplo, los mediáticos exámenes de idoneidad impulsados por Sturzenegger para perseguir estatales.


“Los espacios de formación y el patrimonio del Estado no pueden ser enajenados para negociados inmobiliarios”, sostuvieron desde la seccional porteña de ATE y agregaron: “Defendemos la capacitación permanente, el empleo público y las capacidades necesarias para garantizar un Estado al servicio de la sociedad”.


La venta de bienes del Estado nacional, incluso algunos de ellos de importancia estratégica, ya se convirtió en una peculiaridad de los libertarios. Además del INAP se autorizaron ventas y subastas de terrenos e inmuebles ubicados en Córdoba, Mendoza y Tierra del Fuego.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney accused the Trump administration of issuing demands that would compromise Canada’s sovereignty and undermine key industries. On Saturday, the United States slapped 50% tariffs on around $20 billion worth of imports from Canada, and Carney announced retaliatory tariffs on $20 billion of U.S. products set to go into effect on September 8.

“Canadians are sick of this,” says Avi Lewis, leader of Canada’s progressive New Democratic Party. He says that while the Liberal government has correctly identified voters’ anger, its policies still favor international investors and the fossil fuel industry rather than truly “Trump-proofing” the economy.

author: Battlescarred
title: The 1926 general strike: an anarchist communist critique: ACG Online Public Meeting
content:
Wednesday, September 9th   7 pm – 8:30 pm


A talk and discussion on the history, significance and lessons of the British general strike of 1926 to mark its 100th anniversary


For contemporary anarchists, the General Strike remains highly relevant. It demonstrates that workers possess the capacity to disrupt capitalist society on a massive scale. It also demonstrates that such disruption alone does not guarantee victory. Organisation, political clarity, and democratic control are essential. Movements that rely upon leaders committed to compromise will ultimately be constrained by those leaders’ priorities.


From an anarchist communist perspective, the central lesson of 1926 is that working class power must be organised independently and consciously. At a rank and file level, trade unions can play a role in defending immediate interests, but they cannot be treated as vehicles for the defence of the interests of the working class, of social revolution. Revolutionary transformation requires organisations rooted in the working class yet committed to broader emancipatory goals. It requires structures of direct democracy capable of replacing hierarchical institutions. Most importantly, it requires revolutionary militants prepared to coordinate efforts across workplaces and communities while remaining accountable to those they seek to organise alongside.


For anarchist communists, the defeat of 1926 was not evidence that revolutionary change is impossible. Rather, it was evidence that revolutionary potential must be matched by revolutionary organisation. Without that combination, even the most impressive demonstrations of working-class power can be contained, redirected, and ultimately defeated.

author: Joe Todd
title: Whatever Happened to the ‘Enough Is Enough’ Campaign?
content:
On Wednesday 7 September 2022, Glasgow’s Old Fruitmarket was packed out. Hundreds of people had queued around the block for the city’s biggest leftwing rally in years.


Mark Thomas, a local homelessness worker, remembered being excited.


“It was absolutely massive… It was something new,” he told Novara Media. “[The crowd] was a real mix. Young people who I’d never seen before.”


That September was the end of the UK’s

hot strike summer

. Inflation was skyrocketing, wages were collapsing and energy bills were set to triple. Hundreds of thousands had gone on strike: rail, mail, telecoms and port workers and more. Mick Lynch, the straight-talking former leader of the National Union of Rail, Maritime and Transport Workers (RMT), had spent the summer

going viral

, making the case for striking workers and skewering journalists on live TV.


Amid this crisis, a new campaign was born:

Enough Is Enough

.


Launched in August, Enough Is Enough promised to “turn anger” at the cost of living crisis “into action”. It was, by any measure, an overnight sensation.

150,000 people

 signed up on the first day alone;

450,000

 by a fortnight later. Tens of thousands attended rallies nationwide, wanting to hear how to join a political movement to “win back dignity for working class people”.


But just a few months later, Enough Is Enough went pretty much silent. No more rallies. No more speeches. Just the odd post from a Twitter account. The most dynamic new campaign on the UK left had disappeared – and no-one seemed to know why.


“It feels like a missed opportunity,” said Thomas. “I felt annoyed. What was the point? Was it just a mailing list?”


Four years on, Novara Media spoke to nine co-founders, coordinating group members, organisers and key stakeholders – some of whom chose not to be named to protect their professional relationships – to find out what happened. Their recollections paint a picture of overwhelm, strategic contradiction and a desire for total control. Enough Is Enough didn’t collapse by accident: it was undone by the very organisations that created it.

 


‘We had a platform to create solidarity.’


Wind back to February 2022, and the pressure on the government was building. Prime minister Boris Johnson was flailing in the aftermath of ‘partygate’. Keir Starmer, leader of the opposition, was busy purging the Labour left. There was a political vacuum – and the cost of living crisis was only intensifying.


Chris Webb, then head of communications at the Communication Workers Union (CWU), told Novara Media it was clear working people “were pissed off” and something needed to be done.


That spring, in London pubs and Manchester curry houses, a small group of people hatched a plan. Led by an initial coordinating group made up of Webb, Chloe Koffman (another former staffer at the CWU), Ronan Burtenshaw and Marcus Barnett (then both editors of the socialist magazine Tribune), a meeting was held in London with representatives from Unite and the GMB, as well as Labour councillors, the staffers of leftwing Labour MPs, and Acorn, the community union.


The group shared a sense of urgency about the need to address the cost of living crisis, as well as a desire to reboot Labour party politics. They also didn’t want to become “just another lefty cultural campaign,” according to another co-founder, who chose not to be named.


“The People’s Assembly [another campaign group] was putting on yellow jacket demonstrations in Liverpool that were attracting 25 people,” they told Novara Media.

Don’t Pay

, a campaign that signed up

more than 100,000 people

 to stop paying energy bills and was described by energy firm E.ON as an

“existential threat”

 to the sector was, they argued, also “going nowhere”.


The coordinating group soon agreed on some core demands for the campaign: a real pay rise, a cut in energy bills, an end to food poverty, decent homes for all, and a tax on the rich. What they didn’t have, however, was a collective vision for what the campaign would actually be.


According to one co-founder, Burtenshaw wanted “big names and big tweets” to build a media network, while representatives from trade unions wanted a “rally front” and a “massive defence force” for striking workers (Burtenshaw didn’t respond to requests for an interview). author: Black Freighter
title: Our Dogmatism and Theirs
content:
A Response to Kazi Tanvir Hossein’s ‘Bolshevik Confusion and the Theoretical Bankruptcy of Anarchists’; his article critiques the International Confederation of Labour on the basis of their solidarity work with a garment worker's union affiliated with the Communist Party of Bangladesh

Kazi Tanvir Hossein’s article ‘Bolshevik Confusion and the Theoretical Bankruptcy of Anarchists’ takes issue with a solidarity campaign conducted by the International Confederation of Labour with the Garments Workers’ Trade Union Centre (GWTUC) of Bangladesh over five years ago. His primary concern is GWTUC’s affiliation with the Communist Party of Bangladesh (CPB), arguing that “for anarchists to support or assist any Marxist-Leninist group essentially means directly opposing the core ideals and free thought of anarchism.” A critique of authoritarian socialism is necessary, but it shouldn’t lead us to create new certainties of our own. Anarchism is not a fixed doctrine; it is a living movement of the working class. In rejecting authoritarian socialism, we cannot withdraw from the struggle of workers who finds themselves (at least for now) within imperfect organisations.

To give some context of the situation, the ICL was approached in August 2020 with a call for solidarity with workers at Dragon Sweaters, a firm in Dhaka under the organisational reach of GWTUC. The ICL is a federation of anarcho-syndicalist and revolutionary syndicalist unions – a definition relevant to this discussion as it makes clear that the ICL is not an exclusively anarchist organisation. In its 2018 statutes, it lists solidarity as one of its core principles, “understood as mutual aid among all working people towards each other.”

The letter received by the ICL arrived in the context of Covid-19 lockdowns, detailing a decision by Dragon’s owners to terminate the majority of workers on their sites without outstanding employment entitlements (severance pay etc). The letter therefore appealed to the ICL to campaign on behalf of those workers against brands partnered with Dragon, including Primark, Zara and New Yorker. In announcing their campaign, the ICL also noted that the workers at Dragon were supported by Auraj, a Bangladeshi anarchist network.

After a brief but intense multinational effort, the ICL announced in December 2020 that the campaign was a success. The exact circumstances aren’t relevant to this discussion, but in January 2021 GWTUC General-Secretary Joly Talukder addressed a letter to the ICL and other supporting unions stating that international efforts “pushed the movement to the victory”. This success led to further collaboration between the ICL and GWTUC, including efforts to raise the Bangladeshi minimum wage for garment workers in 2023.

Hossein argues that the ICL’s decision to campaign and raise funds for GWTUC presents “a profound theoretical contradiction”, given the latter’s affiliation with the CPB:

“On one hand, Leninist parties believe in bureaucratic central leadership and the politics of state capture, while on the other hand, anarcho-syndicalist international networks fight for the establishment of a stateless, decentralized, and independent workers' federation. This contradiction is not merely theoretical; it severely damages the labor movement in practical terms as well.”

According to him, Leninism’s ideological dogmatism is among the “primary obstacles to human free intellect” . To free itself of all constraints, he writes that “kindling the flame of doubt is … the sole tool for liberating thought from any dogmatist and materialist shroud.” The problem with this line of reasoning is that anarchism is not just an abstract philosophical system, but a practical ethic of freedom based in material struggle.

Perhaps the most substantial question that Hossein raises is the level of organisational overlap between GWTUC and the CPB. Talukder and much of the union leadership also hold senior positions within the CPB, raising the legitimate question about whether solidarity with GWTUC strengthens the influence of the CPB. This possibility is not in itself sufficient grounds to condemn the ICL’s campaign, however. While GWTUC’s bargaining power has increased, there is no evidence to suggest that solidarity funds were misappropriated by the CPB’s political apparatus. The question Hossain should be asking is not whether GWTUC is affiliated with the CPB but whether the ICL’s solidarity is strengthening worker’s struggle or the party …

title: Archéologie d'un vrai-faux silence : Michel Foucault, Israël et les Palestiniens [3/3]
content:
Inspirés de longue date par le travail de Michel Foucault

 [

1

]

, les philosophes Alain Brossat et Alain Naze ont enquêté sur le « vrai-faux silence » de l'intellectuel préféré des français autour de la Palestine et d'Israël. La première partie de ce travail est accessible

ici

, la seconde

là

.


On a pu discerner déjà, dans les développements précédents, toute l'importance que revêtent les associations subreptices et les enchaînements tacites, dans l'établissement d'une position durable qui ne s'explicite pas sur un mode plein, mais demeure toujours en creux et ne s'expose au grand jour que par intermittences, « au détour d'une conversation » - ou d'une intervention écrite. Ces passages à l'explicite prennent la forme de « sorties », dans la plus parfaite des discontinuités et c'est donc à ses propres risques que l'enquêteur tente de rétablir de la continuité là où ne sont demeurés que des pointillés, très espacés. Le Petit Poucet Foucault ne nous a pas, ici, facilité la tâche, les petits cailloux blancs qui balisent son parcours dans la forêt (sombre) du conflit israélo-palestinien sont rares et souvent bien cachés. Exemple : dans l'un de ses cours au Collège de France (« Il faut défendre la société »), Foucault affirme (un peu hâtivement) que le socialisme, tant comme doctrine que comme pratique étatique, débouche nécessairement sur le racisme

 [

2

]

. Cette simplification a comme effet que la campagne exterminationniste entreprise par Staline contre les « koulaks » peut être associée aux différentes éruptions d'antisémitisme sous le règne de Staline, notamment l'affaire des « blouses blanches » évoquée plus haut. Du coup se trouve renforcée la suture qui, pour Foucault, rend indissociables l'hostilité au communisme à la soviétique et le philosémitisme alimentant la sympathie pour Israël.


Un nouveau nœud de même espèce se forme à l'occasion de l'Affaire Croissant, en 1977. Klaus Croissant, avocat de la défense lors du procès de la Fraction Armée Rouge (« Bande à Baader ») venait de demander l'asile en France, se réclamant de l'article de la Constitution de 1946, garantissant l'asile à quiconque est persécuté pour ses actions en faveur de la liberté. Mais Croissant était poursuivi en Allemagne sous l'inculpation d'association à une entreprise criminelle – celle de la RAF. De ce fait même, il pouvait se trouver exclu du bénéfice de l'asile. Cependant, comme le relève David Macey, pour ceux qui en France le soutenaient, « son véritable crime avait été d'attirer l'attention sur les conditions de détention dans la prison-forteresse de Stammheim » et qui, en octobre 1977, avaient amplement contribuer à pousser Andreas Baader, Gudrun Ennslin et Jan-Karle Raspe à se suicider. De fait, la décision du Procureur de Karlsruhe d'exclure de Croissant de la défense d'Andreas Baader se fondait sur l'affirmation que l'avocat a « pris part à l'élaboration de l'interview au magazine

 Spiegel

, interview qui fait clairement partie de la lutte révolutionnaire que les accusés continuent de mener de leur détention ». Or, comme le fait remarquer Klaus Croissant, les propos tenus par les prisonniers, et repris dans cette publication, « traduisent la définition politique que la R.A.F. (Fraction Armée Rouge) s'est donnée » ; par conséquent, le fait de « présenter cette définition à l'opinion publique avant le procès est l'un des devoirs de la défense et un droit des accusés » - d'où il suit que le tribunal n'était pas compétent « pour censurer les questions posées par le

Spiegel

 et les réponses données par les accusés »

 [

3

]

.


« Croissant, poursuit Macey, avait déjà fait deux séjours en prison ; on lui avait confisqué son passeport et obligation lui avait été faite de se présenter toutes les semaines au poste de police. Désormais incapable de se défendre en Allemagne, il avait choisi l'exil et espéré poursuivre ses activités en France »

 [

4

]

.


Arrêté fin septembre à Paris, il se trouvait alors sous le coup d'une procédure d'extradition. S'ensuivit une mobilisation impulsée par un groupe de personnalités, exigeant la libération de l'avocat, se réclamant d'une longue tradition en matière de droit d'asile pour des motifs politiques. Foucault ne figurait pas parmi les signataires (Simone de Beauvoir, Sartre, Maurice Clavel, Gilles Deleuze, François Sagan, Georges Kiejman...) mais, selon Macey, « il n'en fut pas moins actif, alors, de diverses autres manières »

]

Pour celles et ceux qui ne connaissent pas l'affaire Budapest, Gino est accusé par la Hongrie – avec une dizaine d'autres personnes – d'avoir participé à des violences contre des néonazis en 2023, dans le cadre d'un défilé d'extrême droite organisé chaque année à Budapest en Hongrie : le «

 

jour de l'honneur

 

» qui réunit environ un demi-millier de nazis, commémore l'alliance entre soldats de la Waffen-

SS

 et militaires hongrois lors du siège de l'armée rouge à l'hiver 1945, lorsque la dictature hongroise était l'alliée d'Hitler. Certaines prétendues victimes sont des militants d'extrême droit de nationalité allemande.


Suite à un premier mandat d'arrêt européen émis par la Hongrie, Gino avait déjà été détenu en France plusieurs mois à partir de novembre 2024. Si Gino et d'autres camarades étaient extradés, ils risquaient jusqu'à 24 ans d'emprisonnement en Hongrie. Après une longue bataille, la cour d'appel de Paris avait refusé cette extradition estimant que les risques de jugement inéquitable et de mauvaises conditions de détention étaient trop importants. Notre camarade avait donc été remis en liberté sous contrôle judiciaire.


Le 16 décembre 2025, Gino a été arrêté par les agents de la Sous-direction antiterroriste de la police judiciaire (Sdat) suite à l'émission par l'Allemagne d'un mandat d'arrêt européen à son encontre et placé en détention. Il ressortira deux semaines plus tard, mais s'en suit un acharnement judiciaire qui n'en finit pas. La cour décide de reporter sans cesse le délibéré concernant le mandat d'arrêt émis par l'Allemagne.

title: “Woke 1” Narratives Suggest the US Was Briefly Ruled by the Left. It Wasn’t.
content:
The US wasn’t remade according to abolitionist or socialist movement demands. Now fascists wield the machinery of power.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

The political pendulum swings, and some people are getting caught up in its momentum. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has been reasonably criticized for her giggly embrace of attacks on “Woke 1” — a made-up era of US politics some commentators are now demanding “accountability” for.

The “Woke 1” framing suggests that the United States was briefly ruled by the left. This fantasy erases MAGA from a moment in history when they controlled the levers of government and terrorized their opponents and those they had scapegoated for a moment of national crisis. In 2020, we saw armed protests against COVID mitigations, attacks on health care workers, the mass amplification of conspiracy theories, Trump’s “LIBERATE” tweets, escalating election denial, and the political trajectory that produced an attempted coup on January 6.

It’s true that 2020 was a year of extremes. Experiencing organized abandonment, being pent up at home to ponder the situation, and living much of our political lives in contentious digital spaces contributed to some rather intense pronouncements and actions. This was true on the right and the left. For many Americans, the murder of George Floyd was a flashpoint — one that demanded a reckoning. Calls for reimagining the social order, including abolishing the police, gained traction. And while some were envisioning a world without rampant state violence, where people’s identities were respected and their basic needs met, others were embracing very different forms of radicalization.

Historically, pandemics have been followed by increased social unrest and political upheaval. Many of us hoped this particular rupture might function as a portal, as Arundhati Roy suggested, opening the way for a leftward shift. For a time, this seemed possible.

I have my political disappointments about that period, but they are not about the things many pundits are seizing upon now, as they demand “accountability” for the social repercussions some people endured for racial insensitivity, transphobia, ableism, misogyny, or sex pest behavior — or for toothless corporate policies and mollifying gestures from Democrats that no one on the left asked for.

But whatever missteps people on the left made during that period — for example, some of us may have been too quick to dismiss potential allies we deemed insufficiently radical — our politics did not become the governing politics of the United States. The left did not take power. In fact, many of us lent our momentum to the Biden campaign as a moral compromise to end the Trump regime. The country was not remade according to abolitionist, socialist, or movement demands. Nor did the left lose two elections to a fascist. The Democrats did.

What failed to regain sufficient public support to hold off fascism was the neoliberal status quo. And today, Democrats are still fighting to keep their party’s politics in the center — a position from which they will either continue to lose, or win and then lose, because they ultimately have nothing transformative to offer in a time of increased economic suffering.

Meanwhile, the right continued on its intensified path, ever-radicalizing, until we wound up here.

I am not minimizing the left’s shortcomings. I happen to think leftist Twitter culture, prior to the Elon takeover and sometimes even after, involved a lot of excesses. (Anyone remember the nice lady who made her neighbor chili?) I sometimes engaged in those excesses. (Though not the chili situation.) I was sometimes targeted because of them. (And my god, that shit was ridiculous.) Some leftists, reasonably aghast at Biden’s role in the Gaza genocide, quite unreasonably minimized the threat of a second Trump administration. That was a mistake, and one that aggravated me to no end, but it’s not the mistake we’re being called “crazy” for.

I have come to accept that people don’t always reach the most sensible conclusions in environments designed to amplify rancor and reward conflict, while bombarding people with more bad news and atrocity than their brains were built to process.

People grow, and movements adjust, based on experience and changing conditions. I have learned a lot in recent years, as I hope we all have.

But I want to call attention to what’s been memory-holed …

author: groundxero
title: They Burned Books Then, They Attack Universities Now: Fascism’s War on Knowledge and  Dissent
content:
They may threaten to ‘sew Jadavpur’s mouth shut’. But a university with thousands of students, teachers and workers cannot be silenced by a threat.


 


By

Tanuj Mullick


 


On 10 May 1933, books were burned by the Nazis in cities across Germany. Known as Die Bücherverbrennung am 10. Mai, the event was not merely the destruction of thousands of books. It was a public political programme aimed at establishing control over knowledge, thought, history and freedom of expression. Books written by Jews, communists, socialists, liberals, pacifists and others who were considered enemies of Nazism were declared ‘un-German’ and thrown into the flames.


 


Nearly a century later, when we look at the events that took place at Jadavpur University on 19–20 August, a question inevitably arises: has fascism changed its methods while continuing to attempt to control knowledge, universities and dissenting voices?


 


On the night of 19 August, BJP MLA for Jadavpur, Sharvari Mukherjee, allegedly issued a call in a video for ‘tandav’ at Jadavpur University. Within a short time of the video going viral on social media and being reported by the news media, at around 12:30 a.m., a mob entered Jadavpur University through Gate No. 4.


 


The mob was carrying ABVP flags, rods and sticks and chanting ‘Jai Shri Ram’. Immediately after entering the campus, they allegedly began vandalism and attempted arson.


 


Videos of the entire episode were subsequently made available by a news outlet called Mrittika TV. The faces of several members of the mob can reportedly be seen in the footage. Students of the university identified most of them as people who were not students of Jadavpur University. The one or two individuals who were recognised as students were identified as members of NSF or ABVP.


 


Among them was Aditya Haldar, a student of the History Department who had recently contested the ICC election as an NSF-supported candidate. Alongside him was Somsurya Banerjee of the Electronics and Telecommunication Department, who is alleged to be an NSF member.


 


Some students who were present on campus found themselves directly in front of the mob. Several of them were reportedly beaten severely. Around thirty students were forced to take shelter inside Aurobindo Bhavan, locking themselves in an attempt to save their lives.


 


The mob allegedly continued its attack for a considerable period. They attempted to set fire to Aurobindo Bhavan, threw chocolate bombs, bricks and water bottles, and continued hurling abuses at the students trapped inside.


 


Here one has to ask a very simple question:


 


How did a mob of this size manage to enter the university at around 12:30 a.m. without facing any resistance whatsoever?


 


Does the university not have adequate security?


 


The available information suggests otherwise.


 


A few months ago, despite protests by several students, the university administration had removed its old security guards and appointed ex-servicemen as guards, supposedly to ensure the safety of students. These guards reportedly check students’ identity cards before allowing them to enter the campus, even during the day.


 


Yet CCTV footage allegedly shows that when a mob of approximately sixty people entered through Gate No. 4 that night, the guards were standing there. They reportedly did not check the identity cards of those entering. Even after the mob entered the campus and began its alleged rampage, the guards did not intervene.


 


The CCTV footage reportedly also shows that, at that moment, a staff member of the English Department, Rasman Kanaujjia, was present alongside the guards at Gate No. 4. He is alleged to be a member of the BJP’s employees’ organisation at the university. Also reportedly present was former Jadavpur University Vice-Chancellor Biswanath Sau, who is known as one of the leading figures of the BJP’s teachers’ organisation at Jadavpur.


 


What were the two of them doing there at midnight?


 


This question alone makes the allegation that the attack on the students was carefully planned particularly serious.


 


After questioning the role of the security guards, one must also question the role of the police.


 


While trapped inside Aurobindo Bhavan, several students reportedly tried to contact the police. According to their accounts, when they identified themselves as students of Jadavpur University, the police allegedly disconnected the calls.


 


Students …

title: The murder of Professor Jason Arday
content:
On Sunday 16 August I joined the vigil for Professor Arday in London’s Trafalgar Square in the summer’s heat, packed tight with thousands of protestors marking their respect, holding bunches of flowers aloft, and placards reading, ‘Rest in Power Professor Jason Arday.’ Heads bowed, hundreds around me in tears – the words of his students unbearable, our anger craving a response. 


Professor Arday is dead. Murdered. Yet again another Black person has been killed – pilloried in a public execution orchestrated by a profoundly racist press, and organised fascists.


The vigil spoke to the structural racism that shaped Professor Arday’s life and death. I was struck by British MP Diane Abbott’s comments on the Black experience in the UK and the racism encountered daily. This daily experience is engrained in British institutions, the press and political life.


His family commented about the outpouring of grief and fury, describing their emotions: ‘The public cruelty Jason was subjected to was too much for any man to bear. The outpouring of love, support, and grief since his death means so much to us. Although it is bittersweet now, kindness is needed in life, not just in death.’


Bittersweet indeed – the kindness, support and grief were essential but too late. 


Professor Jason Arday – the Black professor of sociology at Cambridge University – was hounded to his death by a racist campaign to unseat him from his position. In the 22 days leading to his suicide, there were 249 articles in major newspapers in the UK, continual coverage on TV, radio and blogs. This had followed a repeated effort to undermine Arday since he became a professor at the university in 2023.


The noise from this pogrom – accusing him of plagiarism, lies, bombast, academic fakery – was overwhelming. Many people who should have known better joined the chorus. The UK’s mainstream liberal paper, 

The Guardian,

 

launched an investigation into Arday’s scholarship

. I encountered family members who joined in the chorus – denouncing Arday, ridiculing his claims, and his work.


On 5 August, Arday resigned from his post; the following week, on 14 August, he committed suicide. A man described by his students as ‘gentle’, ‘caring’, ‘compassionate’ and ‘inspiring’ was systematically broken – destroyed in a campaign which led directly to his suicide. 


Arday was murdered. 


This was the objective – Arday’s suicide was the logical outcome. Leading the recent crusade was the racist scholar, Nathan Cofnas, who published on his Substack the blog, ‘

DEI Fraud and Cover-Up at Cambridge

’, on 21 July 2026.  A vile man who targeted and conducted his own investigation into Arday’s work  – charging him with plagiarism, which confirmed Cofnas’ thesis that Black people are inferior, unworthy of senior academic positions. 


Cofnas is a symptom of our times. A marginal, bigoted voice that once would have remained largely undetected in the swamp is now amplified by a mainstream, racist agenda. In the global North, these voices have reached fever pitch – finding traction in a political climate that has seen right-wing governments elected, and racist policies normalised in daily political speech. 


To say these developments are worrying is a grotesque understatement – these are clarion signs of our current and deepening crisis, and the irredeemable racism of our political and economic system. This cannot be absorbed and understood simply as a British thing. We see the same tightening of the screw in the personal attacks on International Criminal Court judges and the normalisation of genocide.


There are three observations that I want to make in this piece. Firstly, I want to look at two political parallels –  one that prompted the global mass movement, Black Lives Matter, a few years ago, and the second when antisemitism was denounced by the French author Émile Zola at the end of the 19

th

 century. Finally, I want to say a few things about plagiarism and academia. 


On 25 May 2020 in Minneapolis, George Floyd was stopped by the police, then wrestled to the ground by police officer Derek Chauvin – clips of his slow death over nine minutes were beamed across the planet. Chauvin was later convicted of murder. George Floyd was choked to death by Chauvin, who pinned Floyd to the ground, as he died – filmed by the incredibly brave 17-year-old Darnella Frazie – he was heard saying,‘Mama, mama, mama’, ‘Momma, I love you,’ and ‘Momma! I’m through.’

title: Old traditions of anti-Catholic hate lie beneath UK race riots
content:
Summers in Britain now follow a predictable pattern. 

Southport, England, 2024—racist riots spread after far-right activists falsely blame a stabbing attack on an “illegal Muslim immigrant”. 

Trafalgar Square, London, 2025—anti-Islam hatemonger Tommy Robinson leads the country’s largest ever anti-immigration march after months of rolling protests target refugees and demand mass deportations. 

Belfast, Northern Ireland, 2026—arson attacks, mob violence and protests extend to Scotland and England following a murder committed by a man with Indian heritage.

For three years in a row, Britain has been seized by summertime racist rioting. Islamophobes and nationalists seem to have laid claim to UK streets for the months of June through September. But this is not without precedent: summer has always been high time for bigots and diehard patriots.

It’s the period when Protestant communities in Ireland, Northern Ireland, Scotland and the western part of England habitually mobilise in displays of hatred against Catholics and to show their loyalty to the British state. Colloquially, it has always been “marching season”.

Protestant “loyalism” is a particularly virulent, pro-empire strain of chauvinism that originated with Britain’s historic occupation of Ireland. Beginning in the sixteenth century, English rulers conducted savage campaigns of land confiscation, slaughter and settlement over the whole island. 

British authorities sought to displace local Gaelic-speaking populations, who were largely Catholic. In their place, English and Scottish landlords and aspirational farmers were encouraged to occupy stolen land in resource-rich areas. Catholics were subjected to an oppressive legal regime that denied them the right to vote or hold public office, to own land, to purchase weapons or to freely publish literature. 

From 1690 to 1860, famines and mass evictions of poor peasants from the Scottish highlands compelled large numbers to migrate to the northern part of Ireland. Settlers in the north were explicitly required to adhere to the Protestant faith, speak only English and repudiate any Gaelic heritage they might share with the native Irish population. This was the beginning of the exclusive ethno-religious state that would later become “Northern Ireland”.

Most of Ireland won formal independence from British rule in the 1920s after a particularly fierce decade of revolt against the English crown. But reactionary pro-British capitalists and landowners refused to surrender control of the prosperous industrialised north. They armed and mobilised the Protestant population against the Irish independence movement, deliberately painting a struggle over national liberation in religious colours. In 1921, the British state partitioned the island, granting partial autonomy to a “Free State” in the south (later the Republic of Ireland) but establishing a separate administration in the north-eastern region of Ulster that would remain under British protection.

The modern state of Northern Ireland was officially founded on a two-thirds Protestant demographic majority. This was imposed through tremendous violence. Hundreds of pro-independence Catholics were murdered in Belfast from 1920 to 1922, and 23,000 were hounded from their homes. At least 11,000 Catholic (and many sympathetic Protestant) trade unionists were ejected from workplaces in the north. British troops oversaw mass evictions of Catholic civilians from previously mixed neighbourhoods, and paramilitary brigades of reactionary Protestant settlers were created under British supervision.

Soon after partition, the northern ruling class eagerly agreed to remain under the English crown, joining the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland. Indeed, many northern “loyalists” hoped (and still hope) for a total restoration of British dominance and for the whole island to be ethnically cleansed. It’s this despicable legacy that modern-day loyalism celebrates: loyalty to the British empire, to counter-revolution and to racial supremacy.

This tradition remains one of the key foundations of modern British nationalism. It is not uncommon in Northern Ireland today to see a Protestant child leave the face-painting booth at a summer carnival with the letters “KAT” daubed across their little forehead. “Kill All Taigs” (“Taig” is an ethnic slur for people of native Irish descent) is still a common catch cry alongside “KAC” (“Kill All Catholics”) and “KAI” (“Kill All Irish”) …

title: JinMap and Alo 153 expand mother-tongue services in Istanbul
content:
The Women’s Time Association launched the JinMap application to make it easier for women living in Istanbul to access services addressing violence against women in their mother tongue. Association executive Derya Aslan spoke to JinNews about the initiative. Aslan said the introduction of Kurdish-language services through the Alo 153 support line, following talks with the Istanbul Metropolitan Municipality (IMM), was an important achievement and called for mother-tongue services to be expanded to women’s counselling centres as well.


First digital service of its kind in Kurdish


Aslan said JinMap, developed by the Women’s Time Association, was designed to help women more easily find and access support centres for those subjected to violence. She described it as the first digital mapping initiative of its kind developed in Kurdish and said: “This project showed us how important it is to bring together, on a single platform, the support mechanisms that women need to be able to access easily. Being the first platform of its kind and being available in Kurdish brought us extremely positive feedback. The number of women reaching out for support also increased significantly. This was a very fundamental need.”


JinMap helps women find the support they need


Derya Aslan said JinMap does more than help women locate support centres, explaining that the initiative has also developed into a database providing information on women’s counselling services. Aslan said: “We have also turned it into a database that women can access very easily. It answers questions such as whether there is a women’s counselling centre in their neighbourhood or district, what kind of support that centre provides, where it can refer women for further assistance, and whether its services are multilingual. This came out of the monitoring work we carried out on mother-tongue services.”


Mother-tongue services remain inadequate


Aslan said they contacted all 39 district municipalities as well as the Istanbul Metropolitan Municipality to determine whether services addressing violence against women were available in women’s mother tongues. Their findings, she said, revealed that Kurdish-language services remained severely limited. Aslan added: “Among the 39 districts, only the women’s counselling centres run by Bağcılar and Avcılar municipalities said they provided support in Kurdish. We found that Kurdish was not even on the agenda of the others and that they had no policy on language.”


Istanbul has a large Kurdish female population


Aslan pointed to the large Kurdish female population in Istanbul and stressed the importance of women being able to express themselves in their mother tongue when subjected to violence. She said: “Istanbul is one of the cities with the largest Kurdish populations in the world, and half of that Kurdish population is made up of women. When these women are subjected to violence, they want to tell their own stories and explain what they are going through in their own language. Everyone can express their pain and their experiences much more freely in their own language.”


Kurdish-speaking staff are essential


Derya Aslan stressed that even women who can speak Turkish may struggle to fully express themselves. Aslan said: “Women tell us, ‘I don’t speak Turkish very well, but I can somehow make myself understood. To be able to explain myself comfortably, I used to take my child or someone else with me to accompany me.’ That may no longer be necessary. Having a Kurdish-speaking member of staff there, someone who can listen to a woman in her own language and allow her to express herself freely, would also help build a much stronger relationship of trust.”


Professional Kurdish-speaking staff need to be employed


Aslan described the introduction of Kurdish-language support through the Alo 153 helpline as an important achievement, but said more needed to be done. She continued: “But this alone is not enough when it comes to violence against women. Alo 153 may now provide support in Kurdish, but women’s counselling centres also need to employ qualified professionals who can provide support in Kurdish. We have also called for activities, workshops and training programmes to provide support and services in women’s mother tongues. We have asked for brochures and other public information materials to be made available in Kurdish as well.”


Mother-tongue rights must be part of public policy

author: Katherine Payne
title: African rights advocates coordinate response to family law backlash
content:
24th August 2026


African rights advocates coordinate response to family law backlash


7 min read


News and Insights


Family law


Africa


Campaigners say anti-rights movements are increasingly using family law to challenge women’s rights to inheritance, property, divorce and child custody.


NAIROBI, Aug 13 2026 (IPS) 

– Women’s rights advocates, judges and lawyers have launched a coordinated campaign to reform family laws that discriminate against women and girls in Africa.


While the past decade has brought important legal advances in some countries, progress has also been marked by stagnation and backsliding. Increasingly, influential and often well-resourced and highly coordinated anti-rights actors are promoting regressive conservative ideologies that seek to repeal existing legal protections and obstruct reforms that would strengthen rights for women and girls.


Family law governs some of the most consequential aspects of daily life, including marriage, divorce, child custody, inheritance and property rights. Although national constitutions and regional human rights treaties guarantee many protections for women and girls, those guarantees are often undermined by discriminatory legislation, conflicting customary and statutory laws, and weak implementation.


Rights advocates warn that family law has become a key target for coordinated anti-rights campaigns that promote restrictive interpretations of family, gender roles and “traditional values”, because shaping who has rights within the family sets the framework for whose rights are ultimately recognised and protected across society.


“They understand that if you control the family, you control society,” said Irene Mbengue, senior legal officer in the office of the African Commission’s special rapporteur on the rights of women in Africa, in remarks delivered on behalf of Commissioner Janet Ramatoulie Sallah-Njie at the inaugural Africa Family Law Network conference, held in Nairobi, Kenya, from August 4 to 6, 2026.


“If you define who counts as family, who has rights within the family, and who gets to make decisions in the family, you shift the entire social order.”


That struggle is playing out in Uganda, where rights advocates say proposed changes to marriage law could leave many divorced women with little claim to the assets built up over years spent raising children, running households and supporting their families.


Jackie Bless Pinyoloya, Strategic Initiative for Women in the Horn of Africa (SIHA) Uganda country coordinator, explained that the bill does not guarantee equal division of assets acquired during marriage and leaves women to prove the value of unpaid care work when claiming their share.


“At the point of divorce, a woman is told she only leaves with what she financially contributed… But who counts the years she spent caring for the family?” she said.


Pinyoloya said weak enforcement of existing protections also left women vulnerable, with domestic violence cases often being resolved informally by families or community leaders rather than through courts, while low penalties failed to deter perpetrators.


Equality Now’s

2024 regional study on African family laws

 in 20 African countries found that this tension over marital assets extends beyond Uganda. In countries including Kenya, Nigeria and Tanzania, judicial insistence on proving direct financial contribution routinely penalises homemakers, while courts struggle to place economic value on unpaid care work.


The study also found that many countries retain unequal inheritance and property laws, permit child marriage through legal exceptions, do not criminalise marital rape, and continue to recognise customary and religious laws that discriminate against women and girls.


Rehema Namukose, senior regional programme officer for sub-Saharan Africa at Musawah, a global movement for equality and justice in Muslim family laws, highlighted how phrases such as “family values” often raised questions about whose interests and definitions they represented.


“When they throw around these words, you have to also ask yourself, what is the measure of what family is? How are they defining words like family? Values?” she said.


For rights advocates, the argument is not only over individual laws but also over who gets to define the family those laws are meant to protect.

author: Unknown
title: Cinsiyetçi Teknik Direktör'e tepki
content:
Türkiye Futbol Federasyonu 1'nci liginde oynayan Muğlaspor'un geçtiğimiz günlerde basınla tanışma toplantısı vardı. Toplantıda Teknik Direktör Yalçın Koşukavak'ın kadın gazetecilere yönelik cinsiyetçi sözleri tepki topladı. Muğlaspor Teknik Direktörü Yalçın Koşukavak’ın kadın gazetecilere yönelik “Bilsem kısırımı da altınımı da alırdım, gün yapardık” ve “Sizde şimdi soru da yoktur” sözlerine kadın gazeteciler ve kadın örgütleri tepki gösterdi. Muğlaspor Kulübü ise sözlerin “espri amacı taşıdığını” ve bağlamından koparıldığını savundu.


Muğlaspor Teknik Direktörü Yalçın Koşukavak ile 20 Ağustos’ta Muğla’nın Akyaka Mahallesi’nde futbolcular, aileleri, teknik heyet ve basın mensuplarının katıldığı bir kahvaltı etkinliği düzenlendi. Toplantının başında kulüp başkanı ve yöneticiler mekandan ayrıldı. Koşukavak'ın basın toplantısı için hazırlık yapılırken gazetecilerin oturduğu masa teknik direktör için hazırlanmaya başladı. 


Kahvaltığı basın toplantısını 7 kadın ve 4 erkek muhabir takip ediyordu. Koşukavak, sözlerine "Daha önce basın toplantısında bu kadar bayan görmemiştim. Sizde şimdi soru da yoktur. Bilsem kısırımı da altınımı da alırdım, gün yapardık" diyerek başladı.


Etkinlikte yaşananları Mabolla Medya muhabiri Esma Turan; Koşukavak’ın sözlerini ise Bodrum Kadın Dayanışma Derneği’nden Figan Erozan ve Evrim İnan bianet’e değerlendirdi.


Turan: Bu sözleri 'espri' olarak değerlendirmiyorum


Mabolla Medya muhabiri Esma Turan, kahvaltı etkinliğinde bulunan kadın gazetecilerden biriydi. Etkinlik öncesi ve sırasında yaşananları anlatan Turan şöyle konuştu:


“Toplantı öncesinde kulüp başkanı, yöneticiler ve futbolcular ile kahvaltı yapıldı. Kahvaltı sonrasında sadece hocanın açıklama yapacağı söylendi. Aslında bir tanışma ve değerlendirme toplantısıydı. Yalçın Bey ile ilk basın toplantısı ve tanışma olacaktı. Kulüp başkanı ve yönetimi mekândan ayrıldı. Bizim masamız basın açıklaması için hazırlanıyordu. Biz mikrofonları hazırlarken hoca geldi, daha masaya oturmadan ve merhaba bile demeden kısır muhabbetini yaptı.”


Turan’ın aktardığına göre gazeteciler önce ne olduğunu anlamadı, ardından “Biz de gün yapmıyoruz burada” diyerek tepki gösterdi. Bunun üzerine Koşukavak, “Sizde soru da yoktur şimdi” dedi.


Turan, toplantıda yaşananları şöyle anlattı:


“Biz de kaldık, dinledik açıkçası. Ne yapacağımızı bilemedik yani kal geldi o sırada galiba. Sonradan keşke kalkıp gitseydik dedik. Sorularımız vardı, onları da sormadık. Erkek meslektaşlarımız da soru sormadı. Sadece Yalçın Bey konuştu. 7 kadın ve 4 erkekti gazeteciler.”


Tepkilerin toplantı sonrasında gazetecilerin kendi aralarındaki değerlendirmeleri ve konunun haberleştirilmesiyle ortaya çıktığını belirten Turan, “Haber yapmasalar olur mu? Kulübe zarar gelmesin, cumartesi maç var” denildiğini söyledi.


Koşukavak’ı kişisel olarak hedef almak veya Muğlaspor’a zarar vermek gibi bir amaçlarının olmadığını vurgulayan Turan şöyle devam etti:


“Muğlaspor, bu şehrin önemli bir değeri ve hepimiz kulübün başarılı olmasını istiyoruz. Biz orada söylenen sözleri duyduğumuz şekliyle, kayda geçtiği biçimiyle kamuoyuna aktardık.”


Muğlaspor Kulübü’nün olayın ardından yayımladığı açıklamaya katılmadığını belirten Turan, “Sizde şimdi soru da yoktur” ifadesini kadınların mesleki yeterliliğini ve gazetecilik mesleğini cinsiyet üzerinden değerlendiren bir yaklaşım olarak yorumladı.


Kadınları kamusal alandan dışlayan bir pratik


Bodrum Kadın Dayanışma Derneği de sosyal medya hesabından Koşukavak’ın sözlerine ilişkin bir açıklama yayımladı.


Açıklamada, “Bunu bir kişinin nezaketsizliği olarak değil, erkek egemen kurumların kadınları kamusal alandan dışlama pratiği olarak görüyoruz” denildi.


Koşukavak’ın “kısır” ve “altın günü” ifadelerine de tepki gösterilen açıklamada şöyle denildi:


“‘Kısır’ ve ‘altın günü’ üzerinden kurulan alay, kadınların dayanışma pratiklerini ve mesleki kimliklerini aynı anda küçümsemektedir.”


Muğla Barosu ve Menteşe Kadın Platformu: Münferit bir şaka değil


Menteşe Kadın Platformu ile Muğla Barosu Kadın Hakları ve Toplumsal Cinsiyet Eşitliği Komisyonu da Koşukavak’ın ifadelerine ilişkin ortak bir açıklama yayımladı.


Açıklamada Koşukavak’ın sözlerinin “münferit bir şaka” olmadığı belirtilerek şöyle denildi:


“Bu söylem; sporu, basını ve kamusal alanı yalnızca erkeklere ait gören, kadını ev içi rollerle, geleneksel kalıplarla ve edilgenlikle tanımlamaya çalışan ataerkil zihniyetin yansımasıdır.”
